name: Gorlin formula
seoDesc: Gorlin formula: work out aortic valve area (AVA) from the cardiac output and the heart rate. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Give the Gorlin formula calculator the cardiac output, the heart rate, the aortic mean pressure gradient and the systolic ejection period and it returns aortic valve area (AVA). Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Gorlin formula calculator work?
sections.html:
The Gorlin formula calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports aortic valve area (AVA) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the cardiac output, the heart rate, the aortic mean pressure gradient and the systolic ejection period.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Gorlin formula calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Aortic valve area (AVA)=(10 ÷ 443) × cardiac output ÷ (the square root of (aortic mean pressure gradient) × heart rate × systolic ejection period)
Mitral mean pressure gradient=(100 ÷ 142129) × (cardiac output ^ 2) ÷ ((diastolic filling period ^ 2) × (heart rate ^ 2) × (mitral valve area (MVA) ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in square centimeters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Shown in millimeters of mercury, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Flow rate, opening in liters per minute
  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Area, opening in square centimeters
  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Area, opening in square centimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Gorlin formula calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the cardiac output, the heart rate and the aortic mean pressure gradient — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Gorlin formula calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns aortic valve area (AVA), derived from the cardiac output, the heart rate and the aortic mean pressure gradient. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Gorlin formula calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the cardiac output, the heart rate, the aortic mean pressure gradient and the systolic ejection period, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cardiac output in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cardiac output opens in liters per minute and the chip beside it offers 39 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Gorlin formula calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
